text: Baleful means menacing and harmful — full of the threat of damage, like a glare that promises trouble. The “baleful effects” possible this time are the droughts, floods, and hunger a monster El Niño can spread across whole continents.

Parched means bone-dry — land drained of every drop of moisture, or a person desperate for water. It's the key to the article's cruelest twist: rain falling on parched soil can't soak in fast enough, so it sheets off the baked ground and floods the very places praying for relief.

Fodder is food stored up for farm animals — hay, grain, dried grass. Stockpiling fodder and water for livestock is one of the practical ways to soften a coming drought. Figuratively, fodder is raw material that gets used up for some purpose: an embarrassing trip in the hallway becomes “fodder for jokes.”

A whopper is slang for something unusually huge — a whopper of a fish, a whopper of a lie. Forecasters think this El Niño could be a whopper in the record-book sense: warmer than anything measured in 75 years of record-keeping.

Here an “arm” is a branch of a larger organization — the part that reaches out and does one particular job, the way your arm does. NOAA is an arm of the American government; the FAO is an arm of the UN. No actual arms involved.

A phenomenon is something that happens and can be observed — especially something remarkable or not fully explained. El Niño and climate change are the article's two phenomena (that's the plural): separate forces that happen to make each other worse.

Climatic means having to do with climate — the long-term patterns of weather. El Niño is a recurring climatic pattern. Watch the spelling trap: “climactic,” with an extra c, means the climax of a story — a completely different word.

Equatorial means at or near the equator, the imaginary line around Earth's middle where the sun hits hardest. The anchovies vanish from the equatorial Pacific — the warm band of ocean where El Niño is born.

Anchovies are small, salty schooling fish — the kind some people love (and others pick off) on pizza. Peruvian fishermen noticed centuries ago that their anchovies vanished every few years around Christmas; those little fish are how the world's biggest climate pattern got its name.
To decamp is to pack up and leave suddenly — literally, to break camp. Anchovies prefer cool water, so when El Niño warms the Pacific they decamp southwards, taking the fishermen's catch with them.

Modellers here are scientists who build computer models — simplified mathematical versions of the real world used to forecast what it will do next. Most of the world's climate modellers are pointing the same way: toward a record-breaking warm spike. (The double L is the British spelling.)

Long-run means measured over many years, not just this season. Scientists rate an El Niño by how far the water climbs above the long-run average — the normal level — because a raw temperature by itself tells you nothing about how unusual it is.

Unprecedented means never seen before — there is no earlier example (no “precedent”) to compare it to. A rise of more than 2.5°C would be unprecedented in the 75 years scientists have kept records; the current champion, the 1982-83 El Niño, managed exactly 2.5°C.

Sheer here means pure and nothing but — a word used to stress just how much of something there is. The sheer size of the Pacific means a warm patch there is big enough to reshuffle the entire planet's weather. (On a cliff face, sheer means straight-down steep.)

Interconnectedness is the state of everything being linked to everything else. Because the world's weather systems form one connected web, warming a patch of the Pacific can parch southern Africa and drench Central America — effects thousands of miles from the cause.

Redistribution means moving something around so it ends up spread differently — not more or less of it, just in different places. Each El Niño performs a vast redistribution of heat and moisture: some regions get the rain that others lose.

To amplify is to make something bigger or stronger, the way an amplifier boosts a guitar. El Niño doesn't cause climate change — but the two amplify each other's effects, which is how years like 2016 and 2024 smashed heat records and why 2027 could be hotter still.

Pre-industrial means from before the Industrial Revolution — roughly before the 1800s, when humans began burning coal and oil on a huge scale. Scientists use those temperatures as the baseline: saying 2024 ran 1.55°C above pre-industrial levels measures exactly how much we've warmed the planet since.

Variable here means varying — different from place to place rather than one predictable thing. Globally, El Niño always warms; country by country its effects are variable: drought in one region, floods in another. (In the modelling earlier in the article, “variables” are the factors being measured.)

Havoc is widespread chaos and destruction. The strong El Niños of 1997-98 and 2015-16 caused havoc across eastern and southern Africa, Central America and Oceania — failed crops, hunger, and millions of people forced from their homes.

Pasturelands are the grassy open lands where cattle, sheep and goats graze. When drought parches crops and pasturelands together, the human harvest and the animals' food supply fail at the same time — which is what left millions hungry.

The semi-arid ribbon of land running along the southern edge of the Sahara desert, crossing a dozen African countries. It's a fragile in-between zone where one failed rainy season can quickly become hunger — which is why the FAO singles it out as at risk.

Semi-arid means half-dry: not full desert, but land that gets only just enough rain to farm or graze. The Sahel is semi-arid — which is exactly why a small shift in rainfall there can tip whole countries into crisis.

A double-whammy is two blows landing one after the other, each making the other worse. Somalia's forecast is the textbook case: drought until October, then heavy rain until December — which, on drought-baked soil, doesn't mean relief. It means floods.

A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf and one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints. Its blocking has made fertiliser scarce just as farmers facing an El Niño need it most.

Humanitarian means concerned with saving human lives and relieving suffering. A “humanitarian disaster” is a catastrophe measured in hungry, sick, or displaced people — what the European Commission warns could hit countries from Chad to Haiti.

As a verb, to blunt something is to dull its edge — to soften its impact before it lands. The article ends with ways to blunt the coming blow: drought-tolerant seeds, stored fodder and water. But blunting takes preparation, which is why “the time to start is now.”

The arm of the American government (NOAA, for short) that watches the oceans and the atmosphere — hurricanes, sea temperatures, climate patterns. Its June 11th announcement is what made the new El Niño official.
The United Nations' food-and-farming agency, which tracks where the world's next hunger crises are brewing. It issued the June 9th warning that southern Africa and the Sahel are particularly at risk.
The executive branch of the European Union — the body that runs the EU day to day. Here it's the one warning of possible humanitarian disasters across Africa, the Caribbean and South America.
